text:
Nov 7, 1940: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted itself apart in a 40 mile an hour wind and fell into Puget Sound. It was only four months old, and it changed how every major bridge in the world is built.

For years, people crossing the Tacoma Narrows in Washington state had to take a ferry. In the late 1930s, with help from New Deal money, the state finally got a bridge. Its main span stretched 2,800 feet between its towers, making it the third-longest suspension bridge in the world, behind only the Golden Gate and the George Washington Bridge.

The state's own engineer drew up a design with a deep steel truss under the roadway to stiffen it. It was expensive. A famous New York bridge engineer named Leon Moisseiff, who had consulted on the Golden Gate, offered a sleeker and much cheaper design. Instead of a deep truss, the deck would sit on solid steel girders only eight feet deep. The roadway was just two lanes wide. Moisseiff's design won.

The bridge was so thin and narrow for its length that it moved in the wind even before it was finished. Workers building it said they chewed lemons to fight off seasickness. In light breezes the deck rose and fell in long rolling waves, sometimes several feet high. Drivers said the car ahead of them would disappear from view as it dipped into a trough and then rise back up. People called the bridge Galloping Gertie, and some drove over it just for the thrill.

Engineers tried to calm it down with cables tying the deck to concrete blocks on shore. The cables snapped. A University of Washington professor named Frederick Farquharson started studying it with models in a wind tunnel and filming the real thing.

On the morning of Nov 7, a steady wind of around 40 miles an hour blew through the Narrows. The bridge started its usual up and down motion. Then, around 10 a.m., something shifted. The deck began to twist. One side rose while the other dropped, then the reverse, back and forth, with the roadway tilting so far that the lampposts swung wildly. The bridge was closed.

Leonard Coatsworth, an editor at the Tacoma newspaper, was already on it. He'd been driving across with his daughter's cocker spaniel, Tubby. The car started sliding. Coatsworth got out and tried to get the dog, but couldn't. He crawled the rest of the way to the tower on his hands and knees, cut and bleeding, while the road heaved under him and concrete cracked around him.

Professor Farquharson was there filming. He walked out onto the twisting deck to try to rescue Tubby. The terrified dog bit his finger. He had to leave him.

Just after 11 a.m., a huge section of the main span tore loose and plunged about 190 feet into the water. The rest of the main span followed. Coatsworth's car went down with it, with Tubby inside. He was the only death.

The owners of a local camera shop caught the collapse on film. The footage became one of the most famous engineering films ever made. It's still shown in classrooms around the world and was added to the National Film Registry.

There was one more scandal. The bridge was supposed to be insured, but an insurance agent had pocketed some of the premium money and never sent in a policy. He went to prison.

A panel of the best engineers in the country investigated, including Othmar Ammann, who designed the George Washington Bridge, and aerodynamics pioneer Theodore von Karman. Bridge designers had been thinking about the weight a bridge had to carry. Tacoma showed they also had to think about how wind flows around it.

The collapse is often taught as an example of resonance. Engineers today say it was really aeroelastic flutter. As the deck twisted, it changed how the wind pushed on it, and that pushed it to twist even more, feeding itself until the bridge tore apart.

After Tacoma, bridge designs were tested in wind tunnels. The Golden Gate Bridge was stiffened. Moisseiff's reputation never recovered, and he died a few years later.

A new Tacoma Narrows Bridge, much deeper and stiffer, opened in 1950. A second bridge was added beside it in 2007. The wreckage of Galloping Gertie still lies on the bottom of Puget Sound, where it became a home for giant octopuses. It's listed on the National Register of Historic Places, to protect it from salvagers.

Excerpt I liked from The Fountainhead, Ayn Rand:
________________________
   Thousands of years ago, the first man discovered how to make fire. He was probably burned at the stake he had taught his brothers to light. He was considered an evildoer who had dealt with a demon mankind dreaded. But thereafter men had fire to keep them warm, to cook their food, to light their caves. He had left them a gift they had not conceived and he had lifted darkness off the earth. Centuries later, the first man invented the wheel. He was probably torn on the rack he had taught his brothers to build. He was considered a transgressor who ventured into forbidden territory. But thereafter, men could travel past any horizon. He had left them a gift they had not conceived and he had opened the roads of the world.
   That man, the unsubmissive and first, stands in the opening chapter of every legend mankind has recorded about its beginning. Prometheus was chained to a rock and torn by vultures - because he had stolen the fire of the gods. Adam was condemned to suffer - because he had eaten the fruit of the tree of knowledge. Whatever the legend, somewhere in the shadows of its memory mankind knew that its glory began with one and that that one paid for his courage.
   Throughout the centuries there were men who took first steps down new roads armed with nothing but their own vision. Their goals differed, but they all had this in common: that the step was first, the road new, the vision unborrowed, and the response they received - hatred. The great creators - the thinkers, the artists, the scientists, the inventors - stood alone against the men of their time. Every great new thought was opposed. Every great new invention was denounced. The first motor was considered foolish. The airplane was considered impossible. The power loom was considered vicious. Anesthesia was considered sinful. But the men of unborrowed vision went ahead. They fought, they suffered and they paid. But they won.
   No creator was prompted by a desire to serve his brothers, for his brothers rejected the gift he offered and that gift destroyed the slothful routine of their lives. His truth was his only motive. His own truth, and his own work to achieve it in his own way. A symphony, a book, an engine, a philosophy, an airplane or a building - that was his goal and his life. Not those who heard, read, operated, believed, flew or inhabited the thing he had created. The creation, not its users. The creation, not the benefits others derived from it. The creation which gave form to his truth. He held his truth above all things and against all men.
   His vision, his strength, his courage came from his own spirit. A man's spirit, however, is his self. That entity which is his consciousness. To think, to feel, to judge, to act are functions of the ego.
   The creators were not selfless. It is the whole secret of their power - that it was self-sufficient, self-motivated, self-generated. A first cause, a fount of energy, a life force, a Prime Mover. The creator served nothing and no one. He lived for himself.
   And only by living for himself was he able to achieve the things which are the glory of mankind. Such is the nature of achievement.
   Man cannot survive except through his mind. He comes on earth unarmed. His brain is his only weapon. Animals obtain food by force. Man has no claws, no fangs, no horns, no great strength of muscle. He must plant his food or hunt it. To plant, he needs a process of thought. To hunt, he needs weapons, and to make weapons - a process of thought. From this simplest necessity to the highest religious abstraction, from the wheel to the skyscraper, everything we are and everything we have comes from a single attribute of man - the function of his reasoning mind.
   But the mind is an attribute of the individual. There is no such thing as a collective brain. There is no such thing as a collective thought. An agreement reached by a group of men is only a compromise or an average drawn upon many individual thoughts. It is a secondary consequence. The primary act - the process of reason - must be performed by each man alone. We can divide a meal among many men. We cannot digest it in a collective stomach. No man can use his lungs to breathe for another man. No man can use his brain to think for another. All the functions of body and spirit are private. They cannot be shared or transferred.
   We inherit the products of the thought of other men. We inherit the wheel. We make a cart. The cart becomes an automobile. The automobile becomes an airplane. But all through the process what we receive from others is only the end product of their thinking. The moving force is the creative faculty which takes this product as material, uses it and originates the next step. This creative faculty cannot be given or received, shared or borrowed. It belongs to single, individual men. That which it creates is the property of the creator. Men learn from one another. But all learning is only the exchange of material. No man can give another the capacity to think. Yet that capacity is our only means of survival.
   Nothing is given to man on earth. Everything he needs has to be produced. And here man faces his basic alternative: he can survive in only one of two ways - by the independent work of his own mind or as a parasite fed by the minds of others. The creator originates. The parasite borrows. The creator faces nature alone. The parasite faces nature through an intermediary.
   The creator’s concern is the conquest of nature. The parasite’s concern is the conquest of men.
   The creator lives for his work. He needs no other men. His primary goal is within himself. The parasite lives second-hand. He needs others. Others become his prime motive.
   The basic need of the creator is independence. The reasoning mind cannot work under any form of compulsion. It cannot be curbed, sacrificed or subordinated to any consideration whatsoever. It demands total independence in function and in motive. To a creator, all relations with men are secondary.
   The basic need of the second-hander is to secure his ties with men in order to be fed. He places relations first. He declares that man exists in order to serve others. He preaches altruism.
   Altruism is the doctrine which demands that man live for others and place others above self.
   No man can live for another. He cannot share his spirit just as he cannot share his body. But the second-hander has used altruism as a weapon of exploitation and reversed the base of mankind’s moral principles. Men have been taught every precept that destroys the creator. Men have been taught dependence as a virtue.
The man who attempts to live for others is a dependent. He is a parasite in motive and makes parasites of those he serves. The relationship produces nothing but mutual corruption. It is impossible in concept. The nearest approach to it in reality - the man who lives to serve others - is the slave. If physical slavery is repulsive, how much more repulsive is the concept of servility of the spirit? The conquered slave has a vestige of honor. He has the merit of having resisted and of considering his condition evil. But the man who enslaves himself voluntarily in the name of love is the basest of creatures. He degrades the dignity of man and he degrades the conception of love. But this is the essence of altruism.
   Men have been taught that the highest virtue is not to achieve, but to give. Yet one cannot give that which has not been created. Creation comes before distribution - or there will be nothing to distribute. The need of the creator comes before the need of any possible beneficiary. Yet we are taught to admire the second-hander who dispenses gifts he has not produced above the man who made the gifts possible. We praise an act of charity. We shrug at an act of achievement.
   Men have been taught that their first concern is to relieve the sufferings of others. But suffering is a disease. Should one come upon it, one tries to give relief and assistance. To make that the highest test of virtue is to make suffering the most important part of life. Then man must wish to see others suffer - in order that he may be virtuous. Such is the nature of altruism. The creator is not concerned with disease, but with life. Yet the work of the creators has eliminated one form of disease after another, in man’s body and spirit, and brought more relief from suffering than any altruist could ever conceive.
   Men have been taught that it is a virtue to agree with others. But the creator is the man who disagrees. Men have been taught that it is a virtue to swim with the current. But the creator is the man who goes against the current. Men have been taught that it is a virtue to stand together. But the creator is the man who stands alone.
Men have been taught that the ego is the synonym of evil, and selflessness the ideal of virtue. But the creator is the egotist in the absolute sense, and the selfless man is the one who does not think, feel, judge or act. These are functions of the self.
   Here the basic reversal is most deadly. The issue has been perverted and man has been left no alternative - and no freedom. As poles of good and evil, he was offered two conceptions: egotism and altruism. Egotism was held to mean the sacrifice of others to self. Altruism - the sacrifice of self to others. This tied man irrevocably to other men and left him nothing but a choice of pain: his own pain borne for the sake of others or pain inflicted upon others for the sake of self. When it was added that man must find joy in self-immolation, the trap was closed. Man was forced to accept masochism as his ideal - under the threat that sadism was his only alternative. This was the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on mankind.
This was the device by which dependence and suffering were perpetuated as fundamentals of life.
   The choice is not self-sacrifice or domination. The choice is independence or dependence. The code of the creator or the code of the second-hander. This is the basic issue. It rests upon the alternative of life or death. The code of the creator is built on the needs of the reasoning mind which allows man to survive. The code of the second-hander is built on the needs of a mind incapable of survival. All that which proceeds from man’s independent ego is good. All that which proceeds from man’s dependence upon men is evil.
   The egotist is the absolute sense is not the man who sacrifices others. He is the man who stands above the need of using others in any manner. He does not function through them. He is not concerned with them in any primary matter. Not in his aim, not in his motive, not in his thinking, not in his desires, not in the source of his energy. He does not exist for any other man - and he asks no other man to exist for him. This is the only form of brotherhood and mutual respect possible between men.
   Degrees of ability vary, but the basic principle remains the same: the degree of a man’s independence, initiative and personal love for his work determines his talent as a worker and his worth as a man. Independence is the only gauge of human virtue and value. What a man is and makes of himself; not what he has or hasn’t done for others. There is no substitute for personal dignity. There is no standard of personal dignity except independence.
   In all proper relationships there is no sacrifice of anyone to anyone. An architect needs clients, but he does not subordinate his work to their wishes. They need him, but they do not order a house just to give him a commission. Men exchange their work by free, mutual consent to mutual advantage when their personal interests agree and they both desire the exchange. If they do not desire it, they are not forced to deal with each other. They seek further. This is the only possible form of relationship between equals. Anything else is a relation of slave to master, or victim to executioner.
   No work is ever done collectively, by a majority decision. Every creative job is achieved under the guidance of a single individual thought. An architect requires a great many men to erect his building. But he does not ask them to vote on his design. They work together by free agreement and each is free in his proper function. An architect uses steel, glass, concrete, produced by others. But the materials remain just so much steel, glass and concrete until he touches them. What he does with them is his individual product and his individual property. This is the only pattern for proper co-operation among men.
   The first right on earth is the right of the ego. Man’s first duty is to himself. His moral law is never to place his prime goal within the persons of others. His moral obligation is to do what he wishes, provided his wish does not depend primarily upon other men. This includes the whole sphere of his creative faculty, his thinking, his work. But it does not include the sphere of the gangster, the altruist and the dictator.
   A man thinks and works alone. A man cannot rob, exploit or rule-alone. Robbery, exploitation and ruling presuppose victims. They imply dependence. They are the province of the second-hander.
   Rulers of men are not egotists. They create nothing. They exist entirely through the persons of others. Their goal is in their subjects, in the activity of enslaving. They are as dependent as the beggar, the social worker and the bandit. The form of dependence does not matter.
   But men were taught to regard second-handers - tyrants, emperors, dictators - as exponents of egotism. By this fraud they were made to destroy the ego, themselves and others. The purpose of the fraud was to destroy the creators. Or to harness them. Which is a synonym.
   From the beginning of history, the two antagonists have stood face to face: the creator and the second-hander. When the first creator invented the wheel, the first second-hander responded. He invented altruism.
   The creator - denied, opposed, persecuted, exploited - went on, moved forward and carried all humanity along on his energy. The second-hander contributed nothing to the process except the impediments. The contest has another name: the individual against the collective.

ρ = ρₛ + ρₙ

Where vₛ and vₙ represent the velocities of the superfluid and normal components.

As temperature approaches absolute zero, the superfluid fraction approaches unity.

Egypt has raised approximately US$658 million through the initial public offering of Banque du Caire, a state-owned commercial bank, marking the largest IPO in the history of the Egyptian Stock Exchange and a significant step in the country's privatisation programme.

The transaction involved the sale of a 45% stake by Banque Misr, Banque du Caire’s state-owned parent, through an offering of 6.86 billion shares priced at EGP5.30 each. Following strong investor demand, the offer was increased from an initial 30% stake, with Banque Misr retaining 55% ownership.

Investor demand reached approximately US$4.5 billion, representing around seven times the shares available. The institutional tranche was six times subscribed, while the public offering was oversubscribed 27 times.

The offering also attracted participation from two development finance institutions. The International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) each invested US$100 million, bringing their combined investment to US$200 million.

CI Capital Investment Banking acted as Lead Global Coordinator and Joint Bookrunner, while EFG Hermes acted as Joint Global Coordinator and Joint Bookrunner. Baker McKenzie advised Banque du Caire and Banque Misr, with Helmy, Hamza & Partners providing Egyptian legal counsel.

The IPO forms part of Egypt’s broader state asset monetisation programme, which seeks to increase private-sector participation in the economy and deepen the country's capital markets.

I'm reminded of a famous expression: the storm whispers to the warrior that you cannot withstand my strength. And the warrior whispers back: I am the storm.

We are the storm, and our enemies cannot comprehend our strength, our determination, our resolve, our passion.

Our lineage and our legacy hails back to Athens, to Rome, to Philadelphia, to Monticello. Our ancestors built the cities, they produced the art and architecture, they built the industry. Thousands of years of warriors who raised up families, raised up cities, raised up industry, raised up civilization, who pulled us out of the caves and the darkness into the light.

The light will defeat the dark. We will prevail over the forces of wickedness and evil. They cannot imagine what they have awakened. They cannot conceive of the army that they have arisen in all of us. Because we stand for what is good, what is virtuous, what is noble.

And to those trying to incite violence against us, those trying to foment hatred against us: what do you have? You have nothing. You are nothing. You are wickedness, you are jealousy, you are envy, you are hatred. You are nothing. You can build nothing. You can produce nothing. You can create nothing.

We are the ones who build. We are the ones who create. We are the ones who lift up humanity. You cannot defeat us. You cannot slow us. You cannot stop us. You cannot deter us.

You have no idea the dragon you have awakened. You have no idea how determined we will be to save this civilization, to save the West, to save this republic. Because our children are strong, and our grandchildren will be strong, and our children's children's children will be strong.

And what will you leave behind? Nothing. Nothing. To our enemies, you have nothing to give, you have nothing to offer, you have nothing to share but bitterness. We have beauty, we have light, we have goodness, we have determination, we have vision, we have strength.

We built the world that we inhabit now, generation by generation, and we will defend this world. We will defend goodness. We will defend life. We will defend virtue. You cannot terrify us. You cannot frighten us. You cannot threaten us. Because we are on the side of goodness. We are on the side of God.

**360° overview of this conversation space**

This was a long, multi-voice discussion that moved between personal experience, political strategy, national differences, and deeper life philosophy. Several people spoke (primarily one from Georgia with direct protest experience, one from Ohio/US with a mixed Chinese-American family background, and others chiming in on specific countries or principles). The thread never settled into a single thesis; instead it circled a few core tensions.

### Political resistance and “knowing your people”
The dominant thread was how people respond when governments stop listening or become authoritarian. The Georgian voice described a shift from a relatively democratic system to one that passed a “Russian law,” cracked down on peaceful protests, and controlled media and opposition. In that setting, continuous street action (including what they called rebellion) became the remaining check. They emphasized knowing the local mentality—when people will rise, rest, or push—and rejecting both the government and a “controlled opposition.” Similar points were made about Albania (flamingo movement over land sales), Serbia (students building an alternative to the old opposition and winning), and Iran (diaspora warnings ignored, people accepting high risk because the alternative is permanent constraint).

The counter-view from the American side was that tactics must match the system. In a constitutional republic with residual checks, the preferred tools are assemblies that look more like school-board meetings than open street confrontations, formal legal pressure, and redundancy across channels rather than reliance on any single platform. The shared caution was that gathering in large crowds under modern surveillance is high-risk, and that “peaceful” vs. “unruly” is a thin line that can be redefined by authorities.

A repeated idea was that authentic grassroots effort is defined by who still shows up when cameras leave, and that foreign or elite shaping (funding, narrative control, bused participants) is common everywhere but looks different under different regimes.

### Tools, platforms, and propaganda
Several people argued against depending on any one channel—especially social media owned by people who can throttle or rebrand. The practical stance was “use every available tool, archive what matters, and go where your people actually are.” Words and labels were treated as weapons: the Georgian Dream party’s rebrand to “Georgia Strong” was cited as an example of same owners, same project, new name. The flip side was that people who actually live under the conditions can usually tell the difference between real local energy and imported or opportunistic narratives.

### Personal and longer-horizon threads
A substantial stretch was the Ohio speaker’s family story: a father who built a house with bent nails as a child, served in the Navy, used the GI Bill for physics and nuclear engineering degrees, and co-founded a basement company making high-reliability flow meters that later flew on the Space Shuttle; a mother from Chongqing royalty who arrived with silver sewn into clothing, earned chemistry and MBA degrees while supporting sisters, and joined the same self-reliant path. This was offered as an example of the recycler/self-builder mindset that some participants felt is missing today.

From there the talk moved to technology and abundance (homebuilt systems, offline mesh tools, physics as a lifestyle rather than a credential), extended family models beyond the nuclear unit, and the limits of protection. The clearest line drawn was that trying to keep an adult “safe” by removing their agency is possession, not protection; with children the authority is held in trust and is supposed to be temporary.

### Underlying stance
Across the voices there was broad agreement that:
- Constitutions and laws are paper until the people who enforce them choose to treat them as real.
- Different regimes require different intensities of pressure; what works in one place can be suicidal or irrelevant in another.
- Education, local knowledge, and the ability to distinguish propaganda from reality are prerequisites for not being manipulated.
- Comfort (the ability to “just barbecue and be left alone”) delays urgency until the cost lands on children or basic security.

No one claimed a universal playbook. The space stayed in the tension between “use every tool and keep pressure on until conditions change” and “don’t recreate the same cycles, and don’t treat every country as if it has the same institutional margins.” The personal stories and the physics/family digressions functioned as grounding—reminders that the people talking about these fights also come from concrete histories of self-reliance and constraint.

Mad Men

Mad Men is an acclaimed American period drama television series set in a 1960s New York advertising agency, created by Matthew Weiner. It is widely regarded as one of the greatest television shows of all time, focusing on the professional and personal life of the enigmatic Don Draper (Jon Hamm).Mad Men

Overview

Mad Men ran for seven seasons and 92 episodes from July 19, 2007, to May 17, 2015, on the cable network AMC. The show explores the glamorous, ego-driven world of Madison Avenue advertising firms ("Mad" is short for Madison Avenue) while examining the social mores and cultural shifts of 1960s America, including themes of identity, sexism, race, and family.

Main Cast and Characters

The series features a talented ensemble cast that received numerous awards and nominations:

Jon Hamm as Don Draper: The brilliant but troubled creative director and protagonist, known for his charismatic facade and hidden past.

Elisabeth Moss as Peggy Olson: An ambitious secretary who rises through the ranks to become a respected copywriter, challenging gender roles in the process.
Vincent Kartheiser as Pete Campbell: An ambitious and often conniving account executive vying for power and recognition.

January Jones as Betty Draper (later Betty Francis): Don's wife, a suburban housewife who struggles with her identity and the constraints of her era.

Christina Hendricks as Joan Harris (formerly Joan Holloway): The sharp and capable office manager who navigates workplace sexism and eventually becomes a partner.

John Slattery as Roger Sterling: A womanizing, martini-drinking partner at the firm whose old-guard lifestyle clashes with the changing times.

Critical Reception & Awards

Mad Men received widespread critical acclaim for its writing, acting, visual style, and meticulous historical detail. It made history as the first basic cable series to win the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Drama Series, winning the award for four consecutive years (2008–2011). Other accolades include five Golden Globe Awards and a Peabody Award.

Coles used fake discounts to fool shoppers

The Australian Competition & Consumer Commission's chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb has had a major victory, with the Federal Court ruling that Coles had misled consumers with its 'Down Down' price discounts. Coles could potentially faces millions of dollars in fines after Justice Michael O'Bryan found that the discounts on 13 of the 14 items in a sample basket of 'Down Down' promotions were misleading because they had not been sold at the previous price for a reasonable period of time. Mad Men

Mad Men is an acclaimed American period drama television series set in a 1960s New York advertising agency, created by Matthew Weiner. It is widely regarded as one of the greatest television shows of all time, focusing on the professional and personal life of the enigmatic Don Draper (Jon Hamm).Mad Men

Overview

Mad Men ran for seven seasons and 92 episodes from July 19, 2007, to May 17, 2015, on the cable network AMC. The show explores the glamorous, ego-driven world of Madison Avenue advertising firms ("Mad" is short for Madison Avenue) while examining the social mores and cultural shifts of 1960s America, including themes of identity, sexism, race, and family.

Main Cast and Characters

The series features a talented ensemble cast that received numerous awards and nominations:

Jon Hamm as Don Draper: The brilliant but troubled creative director and protagonist, known for his charismatic facade and hidden past.

Elisabeth Moss as Peggy Olson: An ambitious secretary who rises through the ranks to become a respected copywriter, challenging gender roles in the process.
Vincent Kartheiser as Pete Campbell: An ambitious and often conniving account executive vying for power and recognition.

January Jones as Betty Draper (later Betty Francis): Don's wife, a suburban housewife who struggles with her identity and the constraints of her era.

Christina Hendricks as Joan Harris (formerly Joan Holloway): The sharp and capable office manager who navigates workplace sexism and eventually becomes a partner.

John Slattery as Roger Sterling: A womanizing, martini-drinking partner at the firm whose old-guard lifestyle clashes with the changing times.

Critical Reception & Awards

Mad Men received widespread critical acclaim for its writing, acting, visual style, and meticulous historical detail. It made history as the first basic cable series to win the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Drama Series, winning the award for four consecutive years (2008–2011). Other accolades include five Golden Globe Awards and a Peabody Award.

Mad Men

Mad Men is an acclaimed American period drama television series set in a 1960s New York advertising agency, created by Matthew Weiner. It is widely regarded as one of the greatest television shows of all time, focusing on the professional and personal life of the enigmatic Don Draper (Jon Hamm).Mad Men

Overview

Mad Men ran for seven seasons and 92 episodes from July 19, 2007, to May 17, 2015, on the cable network AMC. The show explores the glamorous, ego-driven world of Madison Avenue advertising firms ("Mad" is short for Madison Avenue) while examining the social mores and cultural shifts of 1960s America, including themes of identity, sexism, race, and family.

Main Cast and Characters

The series features a talented ensemble cast that received numerous awards and nominations:

Jon Hamm as Don Draper: The brilliant but troubled creative director and protagonist, known for his charismatic facade and hidden past.

Elisabeth Moss as Peggy Olson: An ambitious secretary who rises through the ranks to become a respected copywriter, challenging gender roles in the process.
Vincent Kartheiser as Pete Campbell: An ambitious and often conniving account executive vying for power and recognition.

January Jones as Betty Draper (later Betty Francis): Don's wife, a suburban housewife who struggles with her identity and the constraints of her era.

Christina Hendricks as Joan Harris (formerly Joan Holloway): The sharp and capable office manager who navigates workplace sexism and eventually becomes a partner.

John Slattery as Roger Sterling: A womanizing, martini-drinking partner at the firm whose old-guard lifestyle clashes with the changing times.

Critical Reception & Awards

Mad Men received widespread critical acclaim for its writing, acting, visual style, and meticulous historical detail. It made history as the first basic cable series to win the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Drama Series, winning the award for four consecutive years (2008–2011). Other accolades include five Golden Globe Awards and a Peabody Award.
